title: Automated Alpha Discovery Under Rigorous Out-of-Sample Validation: A Forensic Study of Trading Signal Search
abstract: We built a system called Alpha Forensics to test a narrow, specific question. Using price and volume derived building blocks only, can automated search discover equity trading signals that survive rigorous statistical and economic scrutiny? We tested three generation mechanisms against the same validation pipeline: random compositional generation, an LLM guided search that reasons over past trial results, and genetic programming that evolves candidate expressions across many generations. We ran these mechanisms on two stock universes, one with 60 stocks and one with 169 stocks, over four years of daily data. No candidate from any mechanism, on either universe, met our full survivor criteria: passing a deflated Sharpe ratio test, showing a statistically significant alpha after controlling for a set of self constructed factor exposures, and being non-redundant with every other candidate already logged. We report this result in detail, including one candidate that came close to passing and the specific reason it ultimately did not. We also document four methodological issues found and corrected during development. Two made the validation pipeline more conservative than intended. One affected an internal diagnostic without touching any survivor determination. One caused a redundancy check to log a misleading reason for a small number of invalidated candidates without changing which candidates were ultimately flagged as survivors. We treat the absence of a surviving candidate, within the specific vocabulary, universes, and time period we tested, as the central finding of this project.
why: Rigorous validation, null results, LLM-guided search, real method.

title: Moral Inflation in Synthetic Investors: When LLM Personas Replace Heterogeneity with Normative Archetypes
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to stand in for investors in surveys, experiments, and product research. The central validity risk may be more systematic than random simulation error: when financial choices carry clear social or moral prescriptions, LLMs may push synthetic investors toward norm-consistent archetypes. We test this possibility in Islamic finance, where formal prescriptions provide an unusually clear benchmark against which simulated behavior can be compared. Seven persona-conditioned LLMs generated 176,229 cleaned responses, benchmarked against 31 human participants on the same eleven-item instrument. Mean alignment is high (r=0.854), but it masks substantial distributional and structural distortion. Average sign-standardized Moral Inflation is 0.53 Likert points, AI response variance is roughly half the human variance, and religion effects are sharply amplified, reaching eta^(2)=0.795 for musharakah endorsement. The LLMs therefore do not simply reproduce investor heterogeneity. They move simulated people toward an idealized normative archetype. Islamic finance supplies the test environment, but the validity problem extends to any behavioral-finance setting in which models can infer how a responsible investor is supposed to act.
why: LLM persona bias finding; actionable warning for synthetic investors.

title: Do Firms' Stock Prices Respond to AI-related Discussions? Evidence from Earnings Calls
abstract: (This paper is written by Wu Shui Tang, Gabriel (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) and Lam Lok Hang, Stephen (Hong Kong Monetary Authority)) In this study, we examined short-run stock market reactions to firms’ AI-related discussions during earnings calls. Using generative AI techniques to analyse globally listed firms’ earnings call transcripts between 2020 and 2024, we found that AI-related discussions were, on average, associated with positive abnormal stock returns. However, this positive response was associated with discussions that conveyed new information to investors. We further documented heterogeneity across firms with positive and negative earnings surprises. Among firms reporting negative earnings surprises, AI-related discussions were associated with positive abnormal returns only when they contained concrete details, such as specific examples of AI applications or quantitative information. This finding is consistent with investors placing greater weight on specific information when evaluating the AI initiatives of firms facing weaker-than-expected current performance. In contrast, among firms reporting positive earnings surprises, market reactions appeared less sensitive to the concreteness of AI-related discussions, possibly because strong current performance increases investors’ confidence in firms’ ability to translate AI initiatives into future gains.
why: Solid empirical work, but incremental signal, no cost discipline.

title: Enterprise AI Agents in Financial Institutions: Architecture, Governance, Security, Risk Management, and Systemic Risk
abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence is extending the role of AI in financial institutions from information generation and decision support toward systems capable of planning, maintaining state, using tools, coordinating workflows, interacting with enterprise applications, and, where explicitly authorized, participating in operational execution. This transition changes the relevant unit of analysis. The trustworthiness of an enterprise AI agent depends not only on the performance of its underlying model, but also on the data, knowledge, memory, tools, identities, permissions, infrastructure, human decision-makers, and other agents with which it interacts. This white paper develops an integrated framework for understanding enterprise AI agents in financial institutions across architecture, governance, security, risk management, and systemic risk. It examines the technological foundations and principal architectural patterns of agentic AI, representative applications across banking and capital-markets functions, and a technology-neutral reference architecture connecting enterprise data, knowledge, orchestration, identity and trust, governance, security, observability, human oversight, compliance, and enterprise integration. Particular attention is given to the institutional distinction between technical capability and decision authority, and to the conditions under which increasingly autonomous execution can remain bounded, observable, accountable, and reversible. The analysis further argues that individual-agent governance is necessary but insufficient as agentic systems become more interconnected. Shared models, providers, knowledge sources, tools, infrastructure, decision signals, and human-control functions may create common dependencies, correlated behaviour, feedback, propagation, concentration, and cascading effects that are not visible through component-level assessment alone. The paper therefore extends the analysis from individual-agent risk toward the governance and resilience of complete enterprise agent ecosystems. Practical implementation principles, future research questions, and a case study of agentic AI for real-time fraud protection at Lloyds Banking Group illustrate how these concepts translate into operational financial environments. The central conclusion is that successful enterprise agentic AI should not be measured by maximum autonomy, but by the institution's ability to combine useful machine capability with bounded authority, reliable evidence, meaningful human oversight, operational resilience, and clear accountability. Within QWave Consult's broader research programme, systemic risk in agentic AI is being pursued as a continuing research direction alongside post-quantum cryptography.
why: Framework paper, no runnable method or dataset.

title: Algorithmic Lending and Financial Fragility
abstract: We develop a model of algorithmic lending in which a FinTech lender uses a neural network and alternative data to screen borrowers. The FinTech competes with a less-informed bank, and borrowers differ in creditworthiness. Low-quality borrowers can manipulate the characteristics observed by the algorithm, which contaminates the algorithm's training data. The resulting feedback loop between the algorithm's learning and borrowers' manipulation incentives can generate multiple equilibria or prevent an equilibrium from existing. With multiple equilibria, identical borrower populations can face different lending standards and default rates, leading to self-confirming algorithmic discrimination. When equilibrium does not exist, lending standards and manipulation can fluctuate over time despite unchanged fundamentals. To improve stability in the credit market, regulators can implement circuit breakers, restrict FinTechs' data choice, and mandate that lending models are benchmarked against less sophisticated alternatives. Regulation focused on the algorithm itself is unlikely to be effective.
why: Theory-heavy, limited empirical grounding, not actionable.

title: Structural and uncertainty-aware return connectedness in a U.S. AI-relevant equity cluster: A Bayesian Structural Markov-Switching Heteroskedasticity VAR Analysis
abstract: AI-related equity valuations increasingly concentrate in a small set of U.S.-listed firms spanning semiconductor design, general-purpose computing, cloud platforms, and enterprise technology. This study examines whether directional return roles within such a cluster can be distinguished without imposing a recursive ordering and without overinterpreting uncertain point rankings. We estimate a two-state Bayesian structural VAR with Markov-switching heteroskedasticity for NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Microsoft, Alphabet, and IBM. Regime covariance shifts provide non-recursive structural identification, while a pre-specified draw-level mapping reports firm-labelled connectedness measures with posterior uncertainty, conditional on identification and eligibility. The long-horizon reference model over 2006–2026 yields total connectedness of about 52%, close to a generalized Diebold–Yilmaz decomposition on the same data. In the post-2020 matched and macro-financially controlled designs, NVIDIA is a sign-stable net transmitter and Intel a sign-stable net receiver at the 95% level; posterior intervals further distinguish large NET point estimates from transmitter or receiver roles that remain sign-stable. State-conditioned estimates show lower total connectedness in the high-variance state, reflecting a larger own-shock variance share under a constant autoregressive matrix. The results provide an uncertainty-aware, model-based map of directional return connectedness in a concentrated AI-relevant equity cluster.
why: Econometric connectedness, unclear what action to take.

title: Closing the Gap: Financial Supervisors’ AI Adoption
abstract: Financial supervisors face a growing capability gap as financial institutions rapidly adopt artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI (GenAI), and emerging agentic AI. This paper examines the state of AI adoption among financial supervisory authorities, the structural constraints shaping adoption, and the implications for supervisory effectiveness. The analysis draws on primary interviews with senior officials from financial supervisory authorities and financial institutions , the GovSpace State of SupTech Survey , the GovSpace corpus of live and emerging SupTech applications , and S&P Global proprietary data and research , complemented by relevant industry and policy literature. This combination of survey, interview, application-level, and financial-sector data provides both a global perspective on supervisory capabilities and a granular view of how AI is being deployed in practice. The research finds that financial supervisors remain substantially behind the financial sector in AI adoption and maturity. While some authorities are advancing toward AI-enabled, risk-anticipatory supervision, many remain constrained by data availability and quality, legacy infrastructure, skills shortages, limited resources, data sovereignty requirements, and institutional requirements for explainability, accountability, and human oversight. The gap is particularly significant as financial institutions increasingly deploy AI in real-time and move toward more autonomous, agentic systems. The paper proposes a maturity framework for supervisory AI adoption and examines how AI is being applied across internal operations, core supervisory functions, and the emerging supervision of AI-driven risks. It argues that closing the gap does not require supervisors to replicate the technology strategies of financial institutions. Rather, supervisors need to develop the data, infrastructure, talent, governance, and institutional capabilities required to maintain sufficient visibility into an increasingly AI-driven financial system.
why: Regulatory adoption survey, not technical contribution.

title: Do Markets Discipline the Adoption of Dangerous Technology?
abstract: We study adoption when technological disaster risk rises with both capability and deployment. Under a common survivable disaster, adopters suffer the same proportional loss as non-adopters. But disasters select high-capability states, precisely where adopters do best, and marginal utility is high in those states, so markets pay for adopters' payoffs. Adoption is therefore a hedge, though no firm avoids the disaster, and the hedging motive raises adoption, which raises disaster probability in turn. Equilibrium deployment exceeds not only its social optimum but the level that would obtain with no disaster risk at all. The hedge depends on the loss being common: damage confined to adopters taxes them directly, and extinction removes the payoffs that make the hedge worth holding, so both restrain adoption instead. Empirically, we find that option-implied tail risk now moves with stock prices in a manner broadly consistent with a potential common AI disaster.

title: Do AI Trading Agents Herd? Experimental Evidence and Financial Stability Implications
abstract: This paper provides micro-foundations for understanding how AI-powered trading affects market dynamics. We conduct laboratory-style experiments using large language models to replicate classic studies on herd behavior in trading decisions. Our results show that AI agents rely less on market trends and more on private information compared with human traders. However, exploring variations in the experimental settings reveals that AI agents can be induced to herd optimally when explicitly guided to make profit-maximizing decisions. In other experimental variations, we show that AI agents are not purely algorithmic, but have inherited some elements of human conditioning and bias.
why: LLM herding experiment, not real market execution.

title: Algorithmic Pricing in Housing Markets: A Case Study on the National Conflict Concerning RealPage
abstract: Algorithmic pricing is prevalently used in modern rental housing markets for its efficiency, data-driven decision making and reduced administrative burdens for landlords. While these systems are marketed as neutral pricing tools, their widespread adoption has raised serious concerns about rent inflation. This report examines these issues through a case study of the controversy surrounding RealPage, within the context of broader antitrust and AI governance debates. The core challenges identified in this conflict are as follows. First, algorithmic rent-setting undermines price competition by allowing landlords to function as a coordinated pricing bloc rather than as competitors. By pooling nonpublic and sensitive data, RealPage’s YieldStar software enables landlords to align rents above competitive levels, imposing direct harms on tenants. Second, such coordination contributes to rent inflation, resulting in displacement and unaffordable housing. Third, although RealPage characterizes its software as “advice” protected by the First Amendment, regulators challenge this, arguing that the system’s design imposes pressure on landlords to accept said “advice.” While there are promising movements at the state level such as California’s Assembly Bill 325 and Senate Bill 763, the overall regulatory response remains fragmented and incomplete. This report underscores the need for enforceable standards that go beyond transparency–we identify the need to establish frameworks that close the information gap for users and mandate meaningful auditing and testing requirements in order to enforce comprehensive protections for tenants against algorithmic rent inflation.
why: Policy case study; no transferable method or implementation path

title: Understanding European electricity market price variation: an analysis using XAI
abstract: The European electricity market is a deeply interconnected system made up of 49 bidding zones spanning 36 countries, where each bidding zone settles at its own price. The complex interactions between neighbouring bidding zones mean that understanding drivers of electricity price variation in any one bidding zone requires an analysis of its connected neighbours as well as an understanding of the zone’s own generation mix. In this work, we present the first analysis to deploy deep neural networks and explainable AI methods across 39 of these bidding zones to understand the drivers of price variation across each bidding zone. Training an individual model for each bidding zone using features from its connected neighbours, we are able to model the relationship between price and the real-time conditions driving the market. Our results show that the prices in many bidding zones are heavily influenced by neighbours, that renewables despite being small components of the mix are leading contributors to the variation in prices, particularly solar. We also identify a number of bidding zones where electricity prices are primarily driven by gas prices. These results show that the European electricity market is currently in a state of flux with two regimes, renewables driven bidding zones and gas driven bidding zones co-existing within the same system.
why: XAI on electricity markets; wrong market, not financial

title: AI-Driven Cost Optimization in Finance and Accounting: A Systematic Literature Review of Emerging Technologies and Applications
abstract: In the field of finance and accounting, there is continuous pressure on reducing costs and increasing precision and speed. AI can help with it, but the current knowledge about where the costs savings lie is fragmented and spread between different disciplines. This systematic literature review aims at presenting how the AI technologies are used for the purposes of optimizing the costs in the fields of finance and accounting. This paper follows PRISMA 2020 protocol. Open access and peer-reviewed papers published mostly during 2021-2026 have been selected using established databases and screening against clearly defined inclusion criteria. Twenty-five papers have been included into the corpus for the analysis. Thematic analysis resulted in the following five themes: intelligent process automation, fraud detection and loss prevention, credit risk assessment, financial reporting and auditing, and generative AI along with emerging technologies related to it. Cost optimization comes from three main sourcesreduced labour cost, avoided losses, and shortened cycle times. In addition, cost optimization can come from increased prediction accuracy only under certain conditions due to the asymmetric nature of the costs. Adoption barriers are high implementation costs, data governance issues, skill gap and lack of model interpretability. The paper provides the comprehensive overview of the use of AI in finance and accounting with the focus on cost optimization and suggests the agenda for future research.
why: Systematic literature review; survey paper explicitly rejected

title: A Comprehensive Review on Boosting General Insurance in Sri Lanka through an Integrated Phygital and Machine Learning Framework
abstract: The general insurance sector in Sri Lanka is navigating a paradigm shift, driven by digital disruption and evolving consumer demands for seamless, omnichannel experiences. The traditional, agent-centric model is increasingly misaligned with the expectations of a digitally-empowered populace, while a purely digital approach fails to capitalize on the trust inherent in human interactions for complex financial products. This comprehensive review paper posits the "phygital" marketing paradigm-the synergistic integration of physical and digital touchpoints-as the optimal strategic response. We systematically analyze the potential of this approach to enhance customer acquisition, retention, operational efficiency, and brand loyalty. The primary contribution of this work lies in proposing a sophisticated, data-driven framework that embeds Machine Learning (ML) as the core intelligence layer of the phygital ecosystem. We provide a detailed taxonomy of ML applications, including supervised learning for predictive customer analytics, Natural Language Processing (NLP) for intelligent virtual assistants, and computer vision for automated claims processing. The paper further delineates a rigorous methodology for model development, validation, and deployment, addressing critical aspects such as feature engineering and model interpretability. A thorough analysis of implementation challenges, encompassing data integrity, algorithmic bias, and organizational change, is presented. By synthesizing contemporary literature with an advanced, practical ML framework, this study provides a definitive roadmap for insurers in emerging markets like Sri Lanka to transition towards an intelligent, resilient, and customer-centric future.
why: Single-country review paper; no generalizable method

title: Human Capital and Access to Technology-Created Opportunities
abstract: Technological change creates new occupations and task domains, yet we know relatively little about who gains access to these opportunities. We examine this question in the context of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on the forms of human capital that facilitate entry into AI-related positions. Using resume and job posting data from Revelio Labs covering the United States between 2020 and 2025, we compare individuals entering AI-related positions with those entering matched non-AI positions. We find that workers in AI-related positions possess more diverse prior work experience and are more likely to enter through internal moves than workers entering comparable non-AI positions. We also find that the relationship between AI jobs and years of experience varies with how central AI is to the position. Workers in positions where AI forms the technical core of the work tend to have less prior experience but stronger formal credentials, whereas workers in positions where AI is more peripheral tend to have greater years of experience. We further show that collaboration demands, information advantages, and firm-specific knowledge help explain these patterns. Together, our findings demonstrate that technology-created opportunities are heterogeneous and that access to them depends on distinct forms of human capital, with rewards varying according to how central AI is to the position’s core work.
why: Off-topic: labor economics, not financial systems.

title: When Solutions Are Abundant but Problems Scarce: AI in the Market for Knowledge
abstract: We study how artificial intelligence affects welfare in general equilibrium when production requires both finding and solving problems. Unsolved problems are unexploited opportunities or unmet needs that agents find in a congested sector. Problems are solved in layered hierarchies in which agents can ask for help. Firms may adopt a replicable AI agent in either activity. AI deployed in solving problems splits the human knowledge hierarchy: greater AI capability affects the layers above AI, whereas lower cost affects the layers below it. Either form of progress can lower welfare by reallocating solvers to the congested finding sector. A tax on finding corrects this distortion; when this is not possible, the optimal tax on AI can be positive or negative, depending on its effect on the congestion externality.
why: Pure general equilibrium theory, no data or path.

title: AI in the classroom: assessing GPTs' capability in undergraduate finance tests
abstract: This study investigates the proficiency of three leading GPTs, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, in answering final-exam questions for an undergraduate course in Financial Markets and Intermediaries, a specialized finance education context characterized by heterogeneous cognitive and assessment demands. Drawing on Bloom's revised taxonomy and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), this study examines whether GPT performance varies across assessment formats requiring different levels of cognitive processing and reasoning. The results revealed significant divergences: Gemini achieved the highest scores, demonstrating strong comprehension and reasoning skills, whereas ChatGPT showed moderate proficiency and DeepSeek underperformed. All models performed better on multiple-choice questions than on open-ended questions, suggesting that GPTs currently perform more effectively in tasks associated with lower-order cognitive processes. Computational questions posed the greatest challenges across all models, supporting theoretical expectations from CLT. The findings contribute to literature on generative AI in higher education showing that GPT proficiency is not uniform across cognitive assessment levels and by proposing a framework linking AI performance to educational assessment theories. Highly proficient GPTs can serve as valuable supplementary tools for students and educators; however, limitations in complex reasoning, computational accuracy, and regulatory interpretation require critical use. Findings should be interpreted with caution given the single-course single-institution setting.
why: LLM benchmarking on finance education; not real financial work

title: When Capital Chooses: Toward a Political Theory of Agentic Capital
abstract: Political economy divides factors of production via agency. Labor acts; capital is acted upon. Artificial intelligence complicates that distinction, as AI agents act, interact, and spawn on their own. They are a form of capital that allocates itself. I call this agentic capital. Agentic capital matters because it has momentous political implications. To see this, recall that political economy asks whether capital tends to concentrate and what happens when it does. We must ask the same question of agentic capital. I argue it concentrates differently. Agentic capital replicates where returns are highest, and returns rise where it organizes into networks of increasing specialization and productivity. That dynamic can tip a market toward the platform its heaviest users favor. I contend that the tipped state is stable. I also argue that such stability poses a problem for political theory: it exposes others to interference they cannot easily escape by exit, the very mark of republican domination. Worse, exposure forms before anyone chooses to dominate. Agentic capital creates those conditions in advance. I use a formal model of concentration dynamics to make my argument. The model suggests that reversing a tipped market is strictly costlier than preventing one. It also implies that concentration issues measurable warnings before tipping occurs. To slow tipping, societies must detect the warnings. Then societies must implement a new kind of predistribution, not of capital shares but of capital use.
why: Political theory, no data, no visible implementation path.

title: A Non-Debt Money Anchored to Realized Value: A Reform Proposal for Dollar Issuance Rules in the AI Era
abstract: The U.S. dollar system has a structural feature that habit conceals: money is created before valueisrealized. The Federal Reserve issues money against promises about the future—the repayment ofTreasury debt, the acceptance of taxes in payment—while the issuance mechanismitself neververifies whether that money ultimately corresponds to value that was actually realized. IntheAIera this feature erupts into four practical problems: the fiscal deadlock and Treasury-debtsustainability (federal debt has surpassed $40 trillion and net interest outlays nowexceedtheentire defense budget, while the labor-tax base is shrinking); the rupture of thelabor→income→consumption distribution channel; the failure of monetarypolicytransmission (after the zero lower bound, the toolkit contains no instrument that acts directlyondemand); and the unaffordability of the survival safety net (64%of adults worryabout affording medical care, while safety-net financing has only two roads—taxes and borrowing—anda shrinking tax base and expanding debt are closing both). This paper proposes the reverse order ofissuance: money is created only after value has been realized. When a verified real goodisdelivered to a verified real consumer, the delivery event itself triggers the issuance of anequal amount of money, and a smart contract completes pass-through distribution to every linkof thesupply chain in the same instant. The entire operating vehicle of this mechanismis a commodityproduction-and-sales information platform with blockchain and the Internet at its technological core: blockchain's tamper-resistance solves the trust problem of information; the Internet'sreal-time transmission solves the transfer problem of information; information credibilityconstitutes the platform's market competitiveness, independent of its monetary function; andmulti-platform competition in the same form guarantees verification quality. This platformis theimplementation foundation of the entire proposal; it does not yet exist and must be built asapioneering project. The paper provides an ontological analysis of money (does it record promisesor facts), a value theory (production is the necessary precondition; demand is the final realizer), and a minimal formal model (five propositions, testable extensions, and a pilot identificationdesign); it further argues that a complete issuance institution must answer three questions—whatto anchor to (which determines how much to issue), who receives the money first (the injection point), and how to distribute (the distribution technology). This proposal'scombination is: a fact anchor; the first holders of new money are producers rather than consumers; and instant pass-through settlement along the supply chain. For the U.S. institutional environment, the paper shows that the mechanism outperforms the status quo on all three purposes of the CBDCprohibition legislation (preventing payment surveillance, preventing bank disintermediation, andpreventing uncontrolled central-bank power), and that the legislative amendment it requires is, inessence, the transposition of a "issuance without asset acquisition" channel that already existsinU.S. law (the Mint deposit channel, 31 U.S.C. §5112) from coinage to fact-anchored issuance. Onthis foundation the paper presents issuance-based designs for three livelihood modules—basicconsumption, healthcare, and housing—that under normal operation guarantee every citizen'ssurvival floor at zero fiscal burden and zero new Treasury debt: the healthcare module moves thepayment function of Medicare, Medicaid, and ACA subsidies—about $2.1 trillion per year intotal—entirely into the issuance channel and opens it to all (asset tests abolished, theprivate-insurance channel preserved); the housing module uses HUD Fair Market Rentsasarea-level ceiling anchors and absorbs the voucher system; the tax backstop in tail years is statedexplicitly as a hybrid structure rather than evaded. The paper further argues: the proposal'spolitical-consensus structure is superior to any tax-or-borrow alternative (no losers; the decisivebattle is decomposed into reversible steps); it lets the U.S. demand side expand in stepwithAIproductive capacity—social competitiveness in the AI era equals the social demand able toabsorbAI capacity, namely population plus innovation, which is precisely the historical corecompetitiveness of the U.S. market; and the dollar's international standing is thereby upgradedfrom "supported by debt supply" to "supported by real demand." All claims in this paper arerestricted to falsifiable mechanism properties; distant institutional forms do not constitute claimsof this paper.
why: Monetary reform theory; off-topic for financial ML practitioner

title: Market Entry Potential for OTOF Gene Therapy in the Gulf
abstract: This independent working paper assesses the potential for market entry by otoferlin (OTOF) gene therapy developers in Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf Cooperation Council. It combines published hearing-loss genetics studies, demographic statistics, trial and regulatory records, and public information on reimbursement and treatment infrastructure. An illustrative incidence model combines citizen births, congenital hearing-loss rates, genetic attribution and reported OTOF shares, while price scenarios explore potential annual market value. The analysis identifies Saudi Arabia as a candidate for further commercial investigation and patient-identification investment. However, the estimates are sensitive to the representativeness of small, selected clinical cohorts and to assumptions transferred between countries. Estimated OTOF-related births are not confirmed treatment-eligible patients, and full-identification revenue scenarios are not sales or profitability forecasts. The paper argues that diagnostic access, referral completion, payer negotiation and competition from existing hearing interventions are central to evaluating entry. It recommends targeted genotyping and validation of the patient pathway before substantial commercial investment. The work uses public secondary sources and does not report a clinical trial or new patient-level research. AI-use disclosure: Generative AI tools were used to assist with source compilation and to critically examine the analysis's assumptions and arguments. AI assistance was also used to draft the submission abstract.
why: Biotech gene therapy; off-topic for finance
